note.paragraph: A random variable is a real-valued function defined on the sample space $S\text{.}$ A discrete random variable is a random variable that takes on at most a countable number of possible values.

appendix_2.paragraph: Only discrete random variables will be considered in this text; random variables that take on an uncountably infinite set of values are considered in advanced courses in probability theory. In Section 10.3, the expected value of a discrete random variable was defined. The expected value of a discrete random variable may also be defined using a function called the probability mass function.

appendix_2.heading: Periodicity as a Class Property
appendix_2.paragraph: In Section 10.4 it was stated that if two states belong to the same communication class, then their periods must be equal. A proof of this result follows.

note.title: Theorem
note.heading: Theorem
note.paragraph: Let $i$ and $j$ be two states of a Markov chain that are in the same communication class. Then the periods of $i$ and $j$ are equal.

appendix_2.heading: Proof
appendix_2.paragraph: Suppose that $i$ and $j$ are in the same communication class for the Markov chain $X$, that state $i$ has period $d_{i}$, and that state $j$ has period $d_{j}$. To simplify the exposition of the proof, the notation $(a^{r})_{ij}$ will be used to refer to the $(i,j)$-entry in the matrix $A^{r}$. Since $i$ and $j$ are in the same communication class, there exist positive integers $m$ and $n$ such that $(p^{m})_{ji} > 0$ and $\left. \text{(}p^{n} \right)_{ij} > 0$. Let $k$ be a positive integer such that $\text{(}p^{k}\text{)}_{jj} > 0$. In fact, $(p^{lk})_{jj} > 0$ for all integers $l > 1$. Now $(p^{n + lk + m})_{ii} > (p^{n})_{ij}(p^{lk})_{jj}(p^{m})_{ji} > 0$ for all integers $l > 1$, since a loop from state $i$ to state $i$ in $n + lk + m$ steps may be created in many ways, but one way is to proceed from state $i$ to state $j$ in $n$ steps, then to loop from state $j$ to state $j$ $l$ times using a loop of $k$ steps each time, and then to return to state $i$ in $m$ steps. Since $d_{i}$ is the period of state $i\text{,}$ $d_{i}$ must divide $n + lk + m$ for all integers $l > 1$. So $d_{i}$ divides $n + k + m$ and $n + 2k + m$, and so divides $(n + 2k + m) - (n + k + m) = k$. Thus $d_{i}$ is a common divisor of the set of all time steps $k$ such that $\text{(}p^{k}\text{)}_{jj} > 0$. Since $d_{j}$ is the greatest common divisor of the set of all time steps $k$ such that $\text{(}p^{k}\text{)}_{jj} > 0$, $d_{i} \leq d_{j}$. A similar argument shows that $d_{i} \geq d_{j}$, so $d_{i} = d_{j}$.
appendix_2.heading: The Fundamental Matrix
appendix_2.paragraph: In Section 10.5, the number of visits $v_{ij}$ to a transient state $i$ that a Markov chain makes starting at the transient state $j$ was studied. appendix_2.heading: Absorption Probabilities
appendix_2.paragraph: In Section 10.5, the probability that the chain was absorbed into a particular absorbing state was studied. The Markov chain was assumed to have only transient and absorbing states, $j$ is a transient state, and $i$ is an absorbing state of the chain. The probability $a_{ij}$ that the chain is absorbed at state $i$ given that the chain starts at state $j$ was calculated, and it was shown that the matrix $A$ whose $(i,j)$-element is $a_{ij}$ satisfies $A = SM$, where $M$ is the fundamental matrix and $S$ is that portion of the transition matrix that governs movement from transient states to absorbing states. The following theorem restates this result, which was presented as Theorem 7 in Section 10.5. An alternative proof of this result is given that relies on the law of total probability.

note.title: Theorem 7
note.heading: Theorem 7
note.paragraph: Consider a Markov chain with finite state space whose states are either absorbing or transient. Suppose that $j$ is a transient state and that $i$ is an absorbing state of the chain, and let $a_{ij}$ be the probability that the chain is absorbed at state $i$ given that the chain starts in state $j$. Let $A$ be the matrix whose $(i,j)$-element is $a_{ij}$. Then $A = SM$, where $S$ and $M$ are as defined above.
